n: After his first speech, the Lord pauses and invites Job to respond.
Will the one who argues with the Almighty correct him? Whoever accuses God should answer now.

f.g: Argues, brings a lawsuit against.
One who criticizes or accuses God.

n: Job answers the Lord directly for the first time.
Job admits he is small and unworthy; he puts his hand over his mouth. The man who once silenced princes (29:9) is now silent before God.

f.g: I am insignificant, of little account — not “wicked.”

f.w: I will lay mine hand upon my mouth

n: He has spoken once, even twice, but he won’t say any more. Job yields, though full repentance comes in 42:1-6.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom (“once… twice”) meaning “I have said enough.”

n: The Lord speaks again from the storm, beginning his second speech.
Again God tells Job to brace himself and answer his questions.

f.w: Gird up thy loins now like a man

n: God names the real issue: will Job discredit God’s justice — condemn God — just to prove himself right? Job can be innocent without God being unjust.

f.g: Annul, overturn my justice.

f.w: wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous?

n: Does Job have an arm like God’s, or can he thunder with a voice like his?

f.g: The arm symbolizes power.

n: Let Job dress himself in majesty, dignity, glory, and splendor — the royal robes of God.
Let him unleash his fury and humble every proud person he sees.

f.g: Bring him down, humble him.

n: Let him bring down the proud and crush the wicked where they stand.
Let him bury them all in the dust and shroud their faces in the grave.

f.g: Wrap them in the hidden place — the grave.

n: Then God would admit Job’s own power could save him. The point: only God can rule the world in justice; Job cannot save himself.

f.w: thine own right hand can save thee

n: God describes Behemoth, a huge beast he made just as he made Job. Many think it is the hippopotamus, described in poetic grandeur as a symbol of untamable strength.

f.g: A Hebrew plural of majesty meaning “the beast of beasts” — possibly the hippopotamus.
Job and Behemoth are both God’s creatures.

n: Its power is in its hips and the muscles of its belly.

f.g: Hips, lower body.

n: Its tail stiffens like a cedar, and the sinews of its thighs are knit together.

f.w: He moveth his tail like a cedar
f.g: Stiffens or sways its tail like a tree trunk.
Thighs (or reproductive organs).

n: Its bones are like bronze tubes and its limbs like iron bars.

f.g: Bronze.

n: It is first among God’s works; only its Maker can approach it with a sword.

f.w: the chief of the ways of God
f.g: Literally “the first of God’s ways” — echoing wisdom in Proverbs 8:22.

n: The hills provide its food, where wild animals play peacefully around it.

f.w: where all the beasts of the field play

n: It lies under lotus plants, hidden in reeds and marshes.

f.g: Lotus plants.
Marshes, swamps.

n: The lotus shades it, and the willows by the stream surround it.

f.g: Poplars or willows along a riverbank.

n: Even if the river rages, it isn’t alarmed; it stays calm though a flood like the Jordan surges against its mouth.

f.g: Better “if the river rages, he is not alarmed.”
Used here as a symbol of a mighty, rushing river.

n: Can anyone capture it while it watches, or pierce its nose with a hook? No human can master it — but God can.

f.g: Better “can anyone pierce his nose with a snare?”
